title: France's autumn of unrest
deck: A school protest became the worst urban violence in years, hit a state that cannot afford to buy peace, and now shapes a presidential election that Europe and Ukraine depend on.

card.headline: France's protests are a cost-of-living and governance crisis that started in a school corridor

keyNumber.label: marched on 17 October; about 2,400 were arrested that day

forYou.line: Expect lane delays through French ports and hubs on strike days; the next is 5 November.
France pays about 1.4 points over Germany to borrow; a Moody's review lands 23 October.
Copycat cost-of-living unrest reached Italy, Belgium and Portugal the same weekend.
The bigger risk is political: a far-right presidency in May 2027 that would cut Ukraine aid and EU contributions.

effects.text: Town halls, shops and transport damaged in Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Lille, Bordeaux, Limoges
About 1,500 shops hit; damage in the hundreds of millions of euros
Interior minister offers resignation; Macron admits intelligence failures
French borrowing premium back near euro-crisis highs; CAC 40 and euro slip
Budget cuts of EUR 54bn now politically harder; deficit likely to overshoot
National strike called for 5 November; more flare-ups likely
Far right strengthened ahead of April 2027 vote; Ukraine aid and EU budget at stake
Unrest spreads to Milan, Brussels, Liege, Lisbon; elections in Italy and Spain exposed
Investors price political risk into core European debt; ECB rescue unlikely

whatHappened: In late September 2026, students at a high school in Creteil, outside Paris, blockaded their school over teacher shortages and decaying buildings. Within two weeks, more than 1,200 lycees had been disrupted and 6,000 people arrested, 87% of them minors.

On 5 October a 15-year-old lost his hand to a police stun grenade in Lens. The next day 250,000 marched. On 17 October, students, unions and former yellow-vest supporters marched together: about 550,000 people, with looting and arson in a dozen cities and roughly 2,400 arrests.
Macron promised a hard line and possible local protest bans, refused his interior minister's resignation, and admitted failures of anticipation and intelligence.
whyItMatters: France is the eurozone's second-largest economy and already its most fiscally stressed large member: debt at 119% of GDP, a deficit of 5.4%, and a 10-year borrowing premium over Germany of about 140 basis points, the widest since the euro-debt crisis.

The government cannot buy peace. Its 2027 budget needs EUR 54bn of savings to hold the deficit at 5%, and the streets are rejecting exactly those cuts. A hung parliament leaves no majority to pass anything.

The crisis lands six months before a presidential election led by a National Rally candidate polling near 35%, who pledges to end funding for Ukraine within six months and cap France's EU contribution.

winners.why: Best placed to sell order; experts expect anger to be channelled toward immigration rather than austerity.
A distracted, cash-strapped France and a rising party that wants sanctions lifted serve the aim of splitting European support for Ukraine.
Safe-haven flows as investors leave French debt.

losers.why: His promise of a reformed, dynamic France looks spent; the state is seen as failing on schools and order.
France committed about EUR 27bn since 2022 and co-leads the Coalition of the Willing; a French retreat weakens EU-level funding most.
About 1,500 shops damaged on 17 October; Carrefour alone had around 20 supermarkets looted.

losers.who: Anyone shipping through France in November
losers.why: Strike on 5 November; customs and rail capacity reduced.

whatsNext: 23 October: Moody's reviews France's Aa3 negative rating.
5 November: five unions strike; students and pensioners invited to join.
November to December: budget votes in a parliament with no majority; censure motions possible.
18 April and 2 May 2027: presidential election rounds.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what do you think is the most likely path to the April 2027 election?
options: Rolling escalation into a social winter
A bond-market crisis forces an emergency budget
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 45%, is a grinding stalemate: flare-ups fade after the 5 November strike, a diluted budget passes late, and the borrowing premium stays stuck between 120 and 160 basis points. Escalation is the second most likely path at 30%.

causes.name: Debt trap
causes.detail: Debt at 119% of GDP, deficit 5.4%; the interest bill rises EUR 12bn in 2027.

causes.name: Political paralysis
causes.detail: Hung parliament since 2024; Macron cannot run again; no bloc can channel discontent.

causes.name: Fraying public services
causes.detail: Four straight civil-service pay freezes; the state seen as failing on basics.

causes.name: Teacher shortages
causes.detail: About 10% of secondary teaching hours went untaught in 2024-25.

causes.name: Crumbling classrooms
causes.detail: 35 to a class, too few chairs, leaks, summer heat.

causes.name: Parcoursup pressure
causes.detail: The university-entry platform seen as opaque and stressful.

causes.name: Force against minors
causes.detail: A 15-year-old lost a hand; 87% of those held were minors.

causes.name: Austerity budget
causes.detail: EUR 54bn plan and a public-sector strike on 1 October.

causes.name: Fuel-price shock
causes.detail: Diesel above EUR 2 a litre since the Iran war began.

causes.name: Coalition widens
causes.detail: Unions and former yellow vests join the students.

stakeholders.name: Emmanuel Macron
stakeholders.wants: Order restored and a budget passed without owning the cuts
stakeholders.leverage: Police, protest bans, appointments; little political capital left
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hard line on violence, small concessions on schools, distance from the budget fight

stakeholders.name: Sebastien Lecornu
stakeholders.wants: A 2027 budget that satisfies markets without a censure vote
stakeholders.leverage: Can offer the left a no-49.3 deal; can be toppled
stakeholders.likelyMove: Dilute the EUR 54bn package and pass it late

stakeholders.name: Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella
stakeholders.wants: Win in May 2027 on order and living costs
stakeholders.leverage: About 35% first-round support; no need to govern now
stakeholders.likelyMove: Call grievances legitimate, blame the far left, promise order

stakeholders.name: Jean-Luc Melenchon
stakeholders.wants: Lead the left into the run-off on the back of the movement
stakeholders.leverage: Street credibility with students and unions
stakeholders.likelyMove: Blame police provocation; risks being tied to the looting

stakeholders.name: Unions and student organisations
stakeholders.wants: School funding, an end to pay freezes, lower living costs
stakeholders.leverage: Strike calls; 5 November is the next test
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep marching through the budget votes

stakeholders.name: Bond investors and the ECB
stakeholders.wants: A credible fiscal path before buying French debt
stakeholders.leverage: The spread; the ECB's never-used TPI tool
stakeholders.likelyMove: Demand a budget first; no rescue without one

stakeholders.name: Moscow and Washington
stakeholders.wants: Russia: a weaker EU on Ukraine. US: a culture-war talking point on migration
stakeholders.likelyMove: Russia courts the far right; US figures amplify the riots

sectors.why: Sovereign-linked; though bank default-swap spreads sit below the sovereign's, a sign of better capital than 2011.
About 1,500 shops damaged on one day; more protest days ahead.
Strike days close customs and cut rail capacity; Louvre and transport blockades.
Demand for private security and riot cover rises; premiums follow.
Safe-haven flows as French debt is sold.
A far-right win would cut French Ukraine aid; other states may need to fill the gap.
The same fuel shock that fed the protests raises their input costs.

dailyLife.effect: Above EUR 2 a litre since March; record EUR 2.41 in September. A 60-litre tank costs about EUR 30 more than in January.
EU food prices rose 34% from August 2021 to August 2026; a French minimum wage buys about 4% less food than it did.
About 10% of secondary teaching hours went untaught in 2024-25; classes of 35 in summer heat.
Strike on 5 November will hit trains and public services; expect closures around protest squares.
French 10-year yields near 4.9%, the highest since the early 2000s, feed into borrowing costs.

scenarios.name: Grinding stalemate
scenarios.looksLike: Weekly flare-ups that fade after the 5 November strike; a diluted budget passes late or by decree; spread stays 120-160 basis points.
signposts: Moody's cuts the outlook but not the rating
scenarios.effectOnWorld: France stays a weak, inward-looking partner; EU budget and Ukraine deals slip to after the election.

scenarios.name: Rolling escalation
scenarios.looksLike: A social winter: students, unions and ex-yellow vests keep marching; government censured or reshuffled; protest bans or curfews.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Copycat unrest in Italy, Belgium, Spain; far-right gains across 2027 European elections.

scenarios.name: Concession reset
scenarios.looksLike: Government buys peace with school staffing money, a softened pay freeze and fuel relief; the movement splinters.
signposts: A funded school plan before end-October
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Calm streets but a wider deficit; markets punish France modestly.

scenarios.name: Market crisis
scenarios.looksLike: Spread spikes toward 200 basis points; Moody's downgrade; emergency budget; ECB debate over its TPI tool.
signposts: Italian and Spanish spreads widen in step
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Eurozone-wide stress test; north-south fight over ECB support; Ukraine funding frozen.

predictions.text: The 5 November strike will be large but smaller than 17 October; violence will concentrate in big-city centres at night.
The budget will pass only in watered-down form, below the EUR 54bn effort, and the 2027 deficit will overshoot 5%.
At least one rating agency will cut France's rating or outlook before year-end.
The National Rally candidate will stay first in polls; law-and-order, not austerity, will dominate the campaign.
Any new oil-price spike from the Gulf war will reignite protests faster than any budget measure.

actions: Add 2-5 days of buffer to lanes through French ports and hubs on announced protest days.
Review French supplier continuity plans; identify single-source parts from France.
Add fuel-surcharge and force-majeure clauses to contracts touching France.
Issue travel and site-safety guidance for French sites.
Watch the French-German spread: above 160 basis points signals escalation; under 125 signals calm.
Treat French sovereign exposure as political risk, not core-Europe risk, until a budget passes.
Do not assume an ECB backstop; officials say conditions for intervention are not met.
Plan around the 5 November strike for travel and childcare.
Expect fuel and food prices to stay high while the Gulf war continues.
Lock in fixed-rate borrowing where possible; yields are at 20-year highs.
Separate order from grievances: prosecute violence, fund the school plan.
Publish the budget's distributional impact to counter the austerity narrative.
Coordinate with Italy, Belgium and Spain on the shared cost-of-living drivers.

analogues.whatFollowed: De Gaulle's party won a landslide in June; fear of disorder helped the right.
Fuel-tax rise scrapped, EUR 10bn in concessions, 2.5% deficit breach; the movement faded but the grievances did not.
Six nights of violence, 3,000+ arrests, no policy change; far right gained in 2024 European elections.
Reform passed by decree; Macron's approval collapsed; hung parliament followed in 2024.

evidence.method: Built from 19 sources opened on 19 October 2026, ranked by tier: official statistics and ministry counts first, wire and established outlets second, market commentary third. Headline figures use tiers one and two only. Scenario probabilities and predictions are the author's judgement and will be graded on the public scorecard as each resolves.
